business.title: A health information analytics framework for identifying autism spectrum disorder risk using parental and developmental data
business.description: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a complex neurodevelopmental condition influenced by genetic, environmental, and perinatal factors. Identifying patterns in parental medical and behavioral histories may help reveal ASD-related risk indicators. This study examines relationships between parental characteristics, health histories, and ASD occurrence using a machine learning–based framework. A multicenter observational design was used to collect data on perinatal parameters, parental medical and behavioral histories, maternal pregnancy factors, neonatal conditions, and child development. A total of around 109 variables were obtained from balanced cohorts of children with ASD and typically developing controls (55 instances in each). Data were preprocessed and analyzed using frequent itemset mining and association rule methods. Participants were further divided into four age-based subgroups. Multiple supervised machine learning models were applied for ASD vs non-ASD classification. Feature selection methods identified key variables distinguishing ASD and control groups. Frequent pattern analysis highlighted maternal psychological stress, environmental exposures, and dietary-related factors as more common in ASD cases. Classification performance was high, with artificial neural networks (98.0%), k-nearest neighbors (96.5%), and support vector machines (95.16%). Parental and perinatal factors showed meaningful associations with ASD, supporting multifactorial risk patterns.

science.title: Effects of a gender-mixed avatar with male and female body halves on gender identity
science.description: Virtual reality can induce ownership of a virtual body unlike the user’s own, enabling exploration of gender identity. Opposite-gender avatars make gender identity more fluid but do not yield a dual masculine and feminine identity. We examined whether a gender-mixed avatar (male right half, female left half) elicits body ownership and promotes acquisition of both gender identities. Twenty participants used gender-mixed, same-gender, and opposite-gender avatars under synchronous and asynchronous movement. We measured ownership and agency by questionnaire, explicit gender roles with the Bem Sex Role Inventory (BSRI), and implicit gender identity with a single-category Implicit Association Test (IAT). Synchronous movement increased ownership and agency, but ownership of the gender-mixed avatar was lower than for the same-gender avatar and below the midpoint. BSRI scores did not change. IAT responses were faster after the opposite-gender than after the gender-mixed avatar, independently of synchrony. The gender-mixed avatar was not experienced as a body of both genders, since its effects did not exceed those of the opposite-gender avatar. As these effects were independent of synchrony, they likely reflect higher-order cognitive processes rather than the ownership illusion. Because the avatar also combined two individuals into an implausible body, conclusions are specific to this implementation.

science.title: Computational framework for quantitative analysis of Streptococcus mutans biofilms using HR-SEM and confocal microscopy
science.description: Biofilms are structured microbial communities whose architecture plays a central role in antimicrobial resistance and persistence. Although high-resolution scanning electron microscopy (HR-SEM) and confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM) are widely used to visualize biofilms, quantitative image analysis remains fragmented and often relies on manual, modality-specific workflows. Here, we present an open-source computational framework for automated quantitative analysis of Streptococcus mutans biofilms that integrates HR-SEM and CLSM within a unified pipeline. The framework combines single-cell morphometry, bacterial surface texture analysis, biofilm surface coverage, intercellular space quantification, and three-dimensional biofilm characterization. Applied to microscopy images of biofilms treated with increasing concentrations of arachidonic acid, the framework identifies dose-dependent changes in bacterial morphology, surface texture irregularity, intercellular space organization, biofilm coverage, and three-dimensional structure. The computational assays that comprise this work enable objective and reproducible assessment of key morphological features of S. mutans biofilm structure, under two foundational modalities in biofilm research—HR-SEM and CLSM. This work highlights the potential of computational image analysis to advance standardized, objective, and reproducible quantitative biofilm research.
